card: Where builders find their trades, what to send them, scripts to copy for the first call, a sum on builder rates versus homeowner work, and how to stay on the list.
title: How to Get Work From Builders: A Guide for Trades
desc: How to get work from builders as a trade in 2026: who to call, what to send, scripts to copy, the rate sum, and how to stay first on their list for more work.

blocks.h1: How to get work from builders, *and stay their first call.*
blocks.lede: To get work from builders, call the person who books trades (the estimator, project manager or site supervisor), send a short pack with your insurance, licence and photos of similar jobs, and ask for one small job to prove yourself. Then be the trade who answers, turns up and finishes. Builders keep the trades who make their life easy, and most of the steady work comes from staying on their list, not getting on it.

What to send, plus scripts for calls, emails and follow ups
A worked sum on builder rates, the paperwork by country, and how to stay first on the list

blocks.html:
How do you get work from builders?

Builders, general contractors and main contractors all have the same problem: they need trades who show up, do good work and do not cause delays. Your job is to prove you are that trade, fast. The route most trades describe in forums looks like this:

  1. Find builders with work coming up, not just any builder. A firm with three houses going up next month needs you more than one that is quiet.
  2. Contact the person who books trades. On small firms that is the owner. On bigger ones it is the estimator, the project manager or the site supervisor.
  3. Send a short pack the same day: insurance, licence or registration, photos of similar work, the areas you cover and how fast you can start.
  4. Ask for a small job or a price on one package. A first job is a test. Pass it and you are on the list.
  5. Be the easy trade. Answer the phone, turn up when you said, keep the site tidy, and tell them early when something changes.

Owners on Reddit and trade forums say the same things again and again. Call the estimators at the firms you want to work for and tell them exactly what work you are after. Look up local building permits to see which builder is on a job, then ask for their estimating team. Visit in person, then follow up with a call and an email. And start with smaller builders, because two or three small ones can keep you busy while the big ones take longer to trust a new name.

Where do you find builders who need trades?

Where to lookWhat it tells youWhat to do
Building sites in your areaWho is building now; the sign on the fence names the builderNote the name, call the office, ask who books your trade
Council permit and planning recordsApproved jobs that will need trades in the coming monthsFind the builder on each approved job and get in early
Trade counters and suppliersWhich builders buy a lot and who is short of tradesAsk the counter staff; they hear about it first
Other trades you trustBuilders who pay well and builders to avoidSwap names; refer work both ways
Bid and tender platformsLarger jobs where builders invite trade pricesRegister for your trade and area, reply quickly
Local builder associations and networking eventsFaces and names behind the firmsGo, bring cards, follow up within two days

Permit records are one of the most useful tools here, and many councils let you search them online for free. A builder who just got a new home approved will need concrete, framing, roofing, plumbing, electrical, plastering and painting in the next few months. If you call before they have booked anyone, you are not asking for a favour. You are solving a problem they already have.

Who should you contact at a building firm?

Calling the main number and asking "do you need any trades?" rarely works. Ask for a person and a role instead:

  • Small builders (one to ten staff): the owner. They price, book and pay trades themselves. Catch them early in the morning or at the end of the day.
  • Medium builders: the estimator for pricing new jobs, and the project manager or site supervisor for who actually gets booked. The supervisor's opinion of you matters more than anyone else's after the first job.
  • Large or commercial contractors: the estimating or procurement team. They usually have a subcontractor registration form and a prequalification process. Ask for it and fill it in that week. Our guide to getting commercial work covers the paperwork they ask for.

Ask one simple question when you get through: "Who looks after booking [your trade] on your jobs?" Then ask for their email and mobile number.

What should you say to a builder? Scripts to copy

The first phone call:

"Hi [name], it is [your name] from [business]. We are a [trade] business in [town], fully insured, and we do a lot of [type of work, such as new home rough ins or bathroom renovations]. I saw you have a job going up on [street]. Are you set for [trade] on that one, or could I send you our details and a price?"

If they say they already have someone: "No problem at all. Most builders I work with like a backup for when their usual trade is booked out. Could I send you our details so you have them for next time?" That second line wins a lot of first jobs, because every regular trade gets busy, sick or goes on holiday sooner or later.

The email to send straight after:

"Subject: [Trade] for your jobs in [area], insurance attached

Hi [name], thanks for the chat today. As promised, attached are our insurance certificate and licence. A few recent jobs similar to yours: [link to your website or photos]. We cover [areas], can usually start within [X] days, and we reply to messages the same day. Happy to price the [street] job or any package you have coming up. Thanks, [name, mobile]."

Follow up after two weeks: "Hi [name], just checking you got our details. If anything comes up where you need [trade] at short notice, I would be glad to help."

Follow up after a month or two: a photo of a job you just finished, with one line. "Just finished this one in [suburb], thought you might like to see the standard we work to." It keeps your name in front of them without asking for anything.

What paperwork do builders ask for?

Builders check you are insured and legitimate before they check your price. Keep these as PDFs in one folder on your phone so you can send them within minutes:

  • USA: a certificate of insurance (COI) showing general liability, workers' compensation if you have employees, often with the builder named as an additional insured, plus a Form W-9 and your state licence number where your trade needs one.
  • UK: public liability insurance, employer's liability if you employ anyone, and registration for the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS). Under CIS, the builder takes 20% from your payments for HMRC if you are registered, and 30% if you are not, according to GOV.UK. Some subcontractors qualify for gross payment status, which means no deduction. Larger firms also ask for risk assessments and method statements.
  • Canada: liability insurance and a workers' compensation clearance letter from your province (WSIB in Ontario, WCB or WorkSafeBC elsewhere). Builders also report what they pay trades to the CRA on a T5018, so expect them to ask for your business number.
  • Australia: an ABN, public liability insurance, your trade licence and a White Card. Builders report payments to contractors to the ATO through the taxable payments annual report, so your details need to be right on every invoice.
  • New Zealand: public liability insurance, your licence or registration where your trade needs one (for example LBP, electrical or plumbing registration), and a health and safety plan. Many sites ask for a Site Safe passport.

Rules change, so check the current requirements with your accountant, broker or the official site for your country before you start working for a new builder.

Builder rates versus homeowner work: is it worth it?

Builders usually pay less per job than a homeowner would. Trades complain about it often in forums. But the headline rate is not the whole sum, because builder work saves you time on quoting, marketing and chasing. Here is an example with made up but realistic numbers for one job that takes 8 hours on site and $200 of materials:

Homeowner jobBuilder job
Price charged$1,200$950
Less materials$200$200
Left for your time$1,000$750
Hours on site88
Unpaid quoting (1.5 hours a quote, win 1 in 3 homeowner quotes; builder sends plans and books you directly)4.50.5
Admin, calls and chasing payment10.5
Total hours13.59
Real hourly rateabout $74about $83

In this example the builder job pays less but earns more per hour, because you are not pricing jobs you never win. The sum flips if the builder pays late, keeps changing the plan, or makes you come back three times because the site was not ready. Run it with your own numbers, in pounds or dollars, and see our guide to pricing a job for how to build the rate in the first place.

Two rules keep builder work healthy. First, do not let one builder become most of your work. If they go quiet or go broke, you go with them. Second, check payment terms before you start. Many builders pay monthly or 30 days after your invoice, so read our guide to contractor cash flow before you take on a big package.

How do you stay on a builder's list?

Getting the first job is the hard part to start with. Keeping the work is where the money is. Builders in forums describe their favourite trades in almost the same words every time: they answer the phone, they turn up, and they do not need chasing. In practice that means:

  • Confirm every booking in writing the day before, and tell the supervisor straight away if you are running late.
  • Check the site is ready before you arrive. A quick text, "Is the frame up and the area clear for Tuesday?", saves a wasted trip for both of you.
  • Get variations in writing before you do them, even a text. "Extra two power points in the kitchen, $180, okay to go ahead?" Arguments about extras end more builder relationships than bad work.
  • Leave the site clean and tell the next trade anything they need to know.
  • Send photos when you finish and invoice exactly the way the builder asks, with the job address and any order number.
  • Be honest about capacity. Saying "I can do Thursday, not Monday" is better than saying yes and not turning up.

After three or four good jobs, ask: "Are there other builders you work with who need a good [trade]?" Builders talk to each other, and a recommendation from one is worth more than any cold call.

Which builders should you avoid?

Not all builder work is good work. Trades warn about the same red flags:

  • No written agreement, or a contract that says you only get paid when the builder gets paid.
  • A long list of trades who "let them down", which often means trades they did not pay.
  • Pressure to start before the price is agreed.
  • Payment that keeps slipping "until next week".

Ask other trades about a builder before you take a big job. Most countries have laws that help trades get paid on construction work, such as the Construction Act in the UK, security of payment laws in each Australian state, the Construction Contracts Act in New Zealand, prompt payment laws in several Canadian provinces and many US states. They differ a lot, so if a builder will not pay, speak to an adviser early. Our guide on getting paid on time has wording you can add to your quotes.

Why builders search your name before they call

When a builder gets your number from another trade, the first thing they do is search your business. If they find a clear website with photos of similar jobs, your licence details and a phone number, you look like a safe bet. If they find nothing, you look like a risk, even if your work is excellent. A simple site with a page for each service and real photos does the job. See what a trade website needs.

This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: List ten builders with work starting in your area from sites, permits and suppliers
Find the name of the person who books your trade at each one
Put your insurance, licence and tax documents in one folder as PDFs
Pick three photos of jobs similar to what each builder does
Call, then email your details the same day
Follow up after two weeks and again after a month with a photo of recent work
Run the rate sum before you accept a lower builder price
Get every variation confirmed in writing before you do it

items.q: How do I get my first job from a builder?
items.a: Call the person who books trades, send your insurance, licence and photos the same day, and offer to be their backup when their usual trade is busy. A small first job done well usually leads to more.

items.q: Do builders pay less than homeowners?
items.a: Usually yes per job, but builder work cuts unpaid quoting and marketing time. Work out your real hourly rate both ways before deciding, and make sure the builder pays on time.

items.q: How do I become a subcontractor for a general contractor?
items.a: Ask the estimating team for their subcontractor registration or prequalification form, send your insurance certificate and licence, and reply quickly when they invite you to price a job.

items.q: What insurance do builders want from subcontractors?
items.a: Usually public or general liability insurance, workers' compensation or employer's liability if you have staff, and sometimes to be named on your policy. Ask each builder for their exact requirements.

items.q: How many builders should I work for?
items.a: Enough that losing one would not empty your calendar. Many trades aim for several builders plus some direct customers, so no single builder is most of their work.

items.q: Is it worth subcontracting to builders when starting out?
items.a: Often, yes. It gives steady work and references while you build your own customers, as long as the rate covers your costs and the builder pays reliably.
